name: bluewater-shorts-33-42
lines: Last night, somebody in your town asked ChatGPT who to hire. It gave three names.
Yours wasn't one of them.
A year ago, six people in a hundred asked an AI where to find a local business.
This year, it's forty five.
And AI doesn't hand out a page of ten. It gives three or four names, and stops.
It reads websites, reviews and listings. Then it picks the ones it can describe.
So if your site doesn't say what you do, where, and for how much, there's nothing to read.
Write it in plain words. Give the machine something to say about you.
One study checked three hundred and fifty thousand business locations.
ChatGPT recommended about one in a hundred of them.
Not because the other ninety nine are bad.
Because nothing clear was written about them, anywhere it looks.
No services listed. No prices. No town names. Reviews that just say, great job.
The one it picks looks boring. A page that says exactly what they do, where, and what it costs.
Boring wins. Be the one it can read.
Your shop phone rings. A calm voice says, I'm Google's AI, calling for a customer.
Most owners hang up. It sounds like spam.
It isn't. In the US, Google now phones local businesses to ask two things.
How much. And how soon.
Then it sends the customer a list of who answered.
Hang up, and you're not on the list.
So decide your answer today. A price range, and your next open day.
The next caller might not be a person. The customer behind it is real.
A reporter asked Google's AI to call nail salons for a price.
Twenty one minutes later, it came back with one answer.
And one line about everybody else. Couldn't reach them.
That's what your customer reads when your phone rings out.
Not closed. Not busy. Couldn't reach them.
A person might call you back. A robot goes to the next name.
So somebody answers every call. Or you're the line that says, couldn't reach them.
You called the customer back in four minutes. Their phone never rang.
New iPhones can screen any number they don't know.
Before it rings, a voice asks you two things. Who are you, and why are you calling?
Say nothing, and the call just dies.
Mumble, and they read a transcript of you mumbling.
So open the same way, every time. Your name, your business, their job.
It's Dee from Northside Plumbing, about the leak you sent us.
Nine seconds. That's the whole pitch now.
The most valuable thing a customer can do for you takes four seconds.
Save your number.
New phones screen callers they don't know. A voice asks who you are, before it ever rings.
A saved number skips all of it. It just rings, with your name on it.
So ask. Before you leave the job, say, save my number. I'm the one who picks up.
Put it on the invoice. Put it on the fridge magnet.
Every saved contact is a call that gets through next year.
Your truck looks great. Your sign looks great. The machine can't see either one.
When someone asks AI for a local business, it reads. That's all it can do.
In one study, more than half of what ChatGPT pulled for local searches came from the businesses' own websites.
So what does yours say?
Welcome. Quality service. Family owned. That describes every business on earth.
Now try this. Drain cleaning in Burnaby, same day, say from one eighty.
One of those can be quoted. Be the quote.
Do this before you put your phone down.
Open ChatGPT. Type, who's the best, your trade, in your town.
Read the names.
If you're there, good. Screenshot it. That's your new word of mouth.
If you're not, look at who is.
Then open their website. I'll bet it says plainly what they do, where, and what it costs.
That's not luck. That's homework you haven't done yet.
Ask a hundred people where they look for a local business.
A year ago, eighty three said Google. This year, seventy one.
Facebook went up. And one answer went from six hands to forty five.
AI.
Nobody quit Google. They just stopped asking in only one place.
So being found isn't one listing anymore. It's the same true story about you, everywhere they ask.
Same name. Same services. Same town. Say it everywhere.
Google's AI doesn't phone every business in town.
It phones the ones that already show up for that search.
So the map decides who even gets the call.
Complete profile. Right category. Real hours. Fresh reviews.
Old advice. New reason.
Because the customer isn't scrolling the map anymore. A machine is. And it stops early.
Be near the top, or you're never asked.
